title: Graphs
summary: A graph stores relationships between nodes. Traversal needs a visited set so cycles do not trap the program.
refresher: A graph has nodes and edges. An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors. BFS usually uses a queue, DFS uses recursion or a stack, and both need a visited set.
refresher_code:
visited = set()
for neighbor in graph[node]: ...

advanced-graph-node-edge.title: Nodes and edges
advanced-graph-node-edge.body: Nodes are the things. Edges are the connections between them.
advanced-graph-node-edge.example: A -- B means A is connected to B
advanced-graph-node-edge.notice: The same idea can model people, courses, pages, or cities.
advanced-graph-node-edge.mistake: Do not treat a graph like a simple line. A node can have many neighbors.

advanced-graph-visited.title: Visited prevents repeats
advanced-graph-visited.body: A visited set remembers nodes already handled.
advanced-graph-visited.example: if node in visited: skip it
advanced-graph-visited.notice: Cycles can send traversal back to the same node.
advanced-graph-visited.mistake: Without visited, a cycle can run forever.

sections.title: Graph shape
sections.summary: A graph is nodes plus connections.

blocks.body: A graph is useful when relationships matter more than order. Friends in a network, prerequisites between courses, roads between cities, and links between pages can all be represented as graphs.

blocks.caption: An adjacency list maps each node to its neighbors.

blocks.title: Read the structure
items: The value is the list of neighbors.
For an undirected graph, A lists B and B usually lists A.
For a directed graph, an edge may go only one way.

blocks.prompt: What does an adjacency list store for each node?
choices: The number of lines in the program
blocks.why: The adjacency list tells you where you can go next from each node.

sections.title: Visited set
sections.summary: Visited keeps traversal from repeating forever.

blocks.body: Graphs can contain cycles. In a cycle, following neighbors can lead you back to a node you already saw. A visited set prevents that.

blocks.title: Mark before exploring
blocks.body: Mark the node visited before exploring its neighbors. If you wait until after, a cycle can pull you back before the mark happens.

blocks.prompt: Why does graph traversal need a visited set?
choices: To avoid repeating nodes and cycles
blocks.why: Visited remembers what has already been handled.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.summary: BFS goes level by level. DFS goes deep first.

blocks.body: Breadth-first search uses a queue, so it processes older waiting nodes first. Depth-first search uses recursion or a stack, so it follows one path deeply before backing up.

blocks.title: Choose BFS or DFS
items: Need shortest path in unweighted steps? BFS is often a good fit.
Need to explore all connected nodes? Either BFS or DFS can work.
Need recursive shape? DFS often reads naturally.
Always include visited unless the graph is guaranteed acyclic.

sections.title: Disconnected components
sections.summary: One start node may not reach the whole graph.

blocks.body: Some graphs are disconnected. That means there are groups of nodes with no path between them. Starting traversal at one node only visits that node's group.

blocks.title: To visit every component
items: Keep a visited set for the whole graph.
If a node is not visited, start a new BFS or DFS there.
Each new start finds one more component.

blocks.title: Plain meaning
blocks.body: A component is one connected group. If the graph has three separate groups, one traversal from one group cannot see the other two.
